message.content:
The “color” of the sea isn’t fixed—it’s a mix of physics, biology, and perspective:

| Factor | How it changes the look |
|--------|--------------------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow water reflects more light → bright blues/teals; deeper zones absorb longer wavelengths so you see darker indigo‑black hues. |
| **Sun angle & clarity** | A clear midday sun gives vivid azure tones; overcast skies make the surface appear muted gray-green. |
| **Phytoplankton / algae blooms** | High concentrations scatter red light less efficiently, giving the water a greener tint—think tropical lagoons during bloom season. |
| **Sediment / turbidity** | Suspended particles add brownish or muddy shades, especially near river mouths or stormy coasts. |
| **Water composition** | Salt content, dissolved organic matter, and even microscopic organisms influence absorption/reflection curves across the spectrum. |

So while we often think of oceans as “blue,” they’re really a dynamic palette ranging from pale turquoise off sandy beaches to deep midnight black at abyssal depths. In everyday life, most people perceive them as various shades of blue because our eyes are tuned to pick up those wavelengths under normal lighting conditions.
